rows: Climbing Up the Beams on the Empire State Building
Lewis Hine climbed the steel frame of the Empire State Building as it rose in 1930 and 1931. He photographed the builders from dizzying angles, showing ordinary workers as heroes.
Would you want to work this high above the ground?
New York City from Above
Skyscrapers, including the shining top of the Chrysler Building, rise above the streets of Manhattan. By 1932 New York had more tall buildings than any other city in the world.
Which building do you think is the tallest?
Castle Geyser Cove, Yellowstone

Ansel Adams photographed Yellowstone's geysers for a US government project that was supposed to produce murals for the Department of the Interior. The murals were never finished, but his photographs are now in the National Archives.
What do you think the steam smells like?
Plaza del Vapor, Havana
Walker Evans photographed the streets of Havana, Cuba, from a rooftop. The picture shows a great square courtyard of apartments and shops, almost like a map.
What can you tell about how people lived from this view?
Taos Pueblo
Taos Pueblo in New Mexico has multi-story adobe homes where people have lived for about a thousand years. Ansel Adams photographed it under a pale sky for a government project.
Why might people build their homes in stacks like this?
Schoolchildren Line Up for Free Lunch
During the Great Depression many families had little money for food, and schoolchildren lined up for free meals. Photographers recorded these scenes to show how hard times were.
How would you feel if you had to line up for lunch like this?
Port Pirie Smelters
Tall chimneys and furnaces rise over the town of Port Pirie, in South Australia, where metals from mines were smelted. Frank Hurley, the explorer-photographer, photographed Australia's industries.
What do you think comes out of those chimneys?
Circus Poster, Alabama
A bright painted circus poster covers a wall in Alabama. Walker Evans photographed signs and posters across the country as a kind of folk art, and the colors burst through even in black and white.
Which performers do you see on the poster?
Bethlehem, Pennsylvania

Rows of workers' houses climb the hill under the stacks of a huge steel mill. Walker Evans photographed American towns in the Depression for a government project, and this one is one of his best-known views.
What would it be like to live in a house in the shadow of a mill?
Relief Checks Being Handed Out
People crowd around a table to collect checks from a government program that helped unemployed workers during the Great Depression. Lewis Hine photographed the New Deal at work.
Why would people need help like this?
Penny Picture Display, Savannah

A studio window in Savannah, Georgia, shows rows of small cheap portraits of local people. Walker Evans loved photographs by ordinary people, and he copied the look of studio displays in his own work.
If you could see just one face here, which would you choose?
Farmhouse Cabin, Hale County, Alabama
Walker Evans traveled to Alabama with the writer James Agee in 1936 to document the lives of tenant farmers. This small wooden cabin is among the pictures from that trip.
What does the cabin look like inside?
Allie Mae Burroughs

Allie Mae Burroughs was a young cotton farmer's wife in Alabama, photographed by Walker Evans. She looks straight at the camera with a calm, tired face. The picture is one of the best-known portraits of the Depression.
What do you think her life was like?
Farmer Walking in a Dust Storm

A farmer crosses his yard in Cimarron County, Oklahoma, as a dust storm blows. In the 1930s, drought and wind turned the Great Plains into a Dust Bowl. Arthur Rothstein photographed the storms for the government.
What would happen to a crop in a dust storm?
Migrant Mother

In March 1936, Dorothea Lange stopped at a camp of pea pickers in California and photographed a woman named Florence Owens Thompson with her children. The photograph went to newspapers, and food was sent to the camp. It became the most famous image of the Great Depression.
What do you see in the mother's face?
Children Playing in the Gutter
Two children crouch in the street playing a game, as photographed by Russell Lee. He photographed small-town life across the US for a government project during the Depression.
What kind of game do you think they were playing?
General Store Interior, Alabama
Shelves of tin cans, flour sacks and cloth fill a country store in Alabama. Walker Evans photographed the things people used every day, as a record of a time.
What can you find to buy in this store?
Bishop Pass, Kings River Canyon
Jagged peaks rise above a barren slope in California's Sierra Nevada. Ansel Adams photographed this region in 1936 for the Sierra Club, whose campaign helped to create Kings Canyon National Park.
How would you climb up those peaks?
Bud Fields, Cotton Sharecropper

Bud Fields was a cotton farmer in Hale County, Alabama. Walker Evans photographed him and his family for the book Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, to show the dignity of people living through hard times.
What can you see in his face?
Stone and William Streets, Manhattan

Berenice Abbott photographed New York for years to record how fast it was changing. She looked down on this canyon of skyscrapers in the Financial District from above, so the buildings tower and cross like angled walls.
How does the high viewpoint make the buildings look?
Dust Storm, Boise City, Oklahoma
A wall of dust blows over a farm in Oklahoma in 1936. Dust storms like this carried topsoil hundreds of miles and forced many families to leave their farms.
How would you protect a house from dust?
Dust Storm Damage, Cimarron County
Drifts of dust bury fences and cover a farm. After years without rain, the soil blew away, leaving farmers with nothing to grow.
How would you clean up after a storm like this?
Hosiery Worker
Hands guide stockings through a machine in a factory. Lewis Hine photographed workers' hands and skills to show that modern industry depended on the people who ran the machines.
What do you notice about the hands in this picture?
